item.description:
• A sitter keeps the way it was put down, and the bowl is aimed past. Two things broke when a sitter's feet were made to stay where it stood and the rest of it put down behind them.
  • The fly-in goes until it is known why a launch drops frames. It read badly however it was driven — eased toward a target, or taken exactly off the clock — and a camera that moves unevenly is worse than one that does not move at all. So the view holds one height on the monolith while the floor arrives, and takes in the whole station once, at the end, which is the part that was working.
  • The disk is not written to during a frame. Saving the floor happens at the end of every redraw, and a launch does a dozen of them while the offices arrive — each one encoding every station and writing it out on the thread that is drawing. Remembering what GitHub said did the same. Both hand the finished bytes to a queue of their own now; the encoding still reads the model, so it stays where it is.
  • The fly-in is read off the clock, with nothing easing toward it. You had it right: the camera settling was the staggering all along, and taking the redraws away only left the settling on its own to be seen.
  • The station is flown in on rather than snapped to. The first frame of a launch framed a fleet with nothing in it, which falls back to six tiles across: a close-up of empty sky and drifting dust, held until the floor turned up and the camera had to travel to meet it.
  • Nobody arrives in formation. A launch put every minion on the floor in the same frame, at the same speed, and sent them all to bed together — four of them lying down in step, which reads as choreography rather than as people.
  • Settled means the rebuilding has gone quiet, not that GitHub has answered. The answers are not the end of a launch: offices land after them and minions after those, each one a rebuild of the floor, so letting the view go when the last repository replied let it go two steps early — the third rebuild jumped it out, and the fourth slid and zoomed it into place.
  • The view is pinned on the monolith while the floor arrives, because there is nothing to compute. Framing the station meant framing its bounds, and its bounds grow with every office; framing only the parts a station always has was no better, since the hallway is among them and the hallway is dug outward as each office is placed. Both were answers to the wrong question. The middle of a station is where it has always been, and a launch does not need a view fitted to a floor that is still changing — it needs one that holds still.
  • The floor is still arriving before it has found anything. `stillLooking` asked whether any known repository was unanswered, and answered no while none were known yet — which is the first second or two of every launch, and exactly the stretch it was written for. So the camera never held, and reframed on every office as it landed. It now counts having found nothing as still looking, bounded by scans so a repository that never answers cannot hold it open for ever.
  • The camera holds on what a station always has, until it knows what else it has. A station's bounds grow with every office that arrives, and the view frames its bounds, so each answer from GitHub moved and rescaled the whole picture under you — seven times over a few seconds while the offices came in.
  • The breathing runs off the wall clock, and the floor settles once it has stopped arriving.
  • Revert "A waiting office is simply dim, and comes up when it has been looked at. The breathing goes. It was tried as an action on the tiles, which begins again with the node it is attached to and so was never seen while the floor was still being built; then from the tick on the station's own clock, which stands still exactly when the floor is being worked out; then on the wall clock, which moves but still showed nothing. Three goes for a flourish on a state that lasts three or four seconds, against a plain dim that reads at a glance and was already doing the job."
  • A waiting office is simply dim, and comes up when it has been looked at. The breathing goes. It was tried as an action on the tiles, which begins again with the node it is attached to and so was never seen while the floor was still being built; then from the tick on the station's own clock, which stands still exactly when the floor is being worked out; then on the wall clock, which moves but still showed nothing. Three goes for a flourish on a state that lasts three or four seconds, against a plain dim that reads at a glance and was already doing the job.
  • Coming up to full is a change of light, not of floor. Confirming a repository redrew the whole station, and measuring a launch showed what that costs: ten redraws in fourteen seconds, four of them while offices were still waiting to be looked at. Every one built the tiles afresh, so the breath began again from nothing each time and was never seen to move, and the floor jumped under everything each time another repository answered — which is the staggering, not the answers arriving.
  • The breath starts at once rather than after a pause. It was put out of step by waiting a moment before beginning, which is the one thing that cannot work here: the floor is redrawn whenever anything about it changes, every redraw builds the tiles afresh and starts the action again from its pause, and an office confirmed within a second or two was never seen to move at all. Rooms are put out of step by where in the breath they start instead, so there is motion from the first frame and no two are in unison.
  • An office not yet confirmed today breathes until it is. Two things were wrong with the first go at it.
  • Last night's floor is drawn low until it has been looked at today. The station now comes back with what it knew, which made everything look certain: a room restored from the floor carries the checkout it had, and a room the cache vouches for carries its pull request, so nothing was provisional and nothing was dim. That is the picture of a station that has been checked, not one that has just woken up.
  • What the cache knows is kept up to date, not just filled in once. It was written the first time a repository answered and never again, so a pull request that went away later in the run was still in it at the next launch: the office came back from the dead each morning, stood dim until GitHub was asked again, and was dropped again. It is written when a repository first answers and every minute after, so an office that has gone from GitHub goes from the floor and from what the next launch is told.
  • The station comes back with what it knew, and the lights come up as GitHub answers. It kept its floor between runs but not a word of what GitHub had said about it, so every launch began by waiting to be told what it already knew — and behind a hold of three to twelve seconds, picked at random so that machines on one network do not all ask at once, which is sound for a five-minute backstop and absurd as the first thing a person waits for.
  • The floor waits once, not once per repository. Offices were held until their own repository had spoken, so they arrived a repository at a time — a few, a long gap, a few more — and the pulse that says the station is waiting stopped after the first answer while most of the floor was still to come. Either the station is waiting or it is not: it holds everything until everything it has found has answered, and puts the floor down in one go.
  • The offices everyone can see go down first. Placement was already deterministic, so that two machines with the same rooms dig the same hallway — but only the order they are added in decides where each one lands, and its cells are then kept. Your own offices were added from the session scan at once and GitHub's seconds later, so the shared ones took whatever floor was left and no two stations looked alike.
  • An office is named by its pull request, once there is one. A branch names it until GitHub says which pull request it is, and after that the pull request does.
  • Three kinds of office, and they do not end the same way. One of yours is backed by a checkout on this disk; one of a neighbour's by their word over the network; one is GitHub's alone. They were all cleared on the same rule — the pull request merged, the crate hauled, the office gone — and for a remote office that is right, because branches are left to die with their pull requests rather than deleted, so the merge really is the last anybody hears of it.
  • The station remembers whose it is. Which GitHub account is signed in is asked by running `gh api user` inside a repository, so it cannot be answered until a repository has been found, and the answer was kept only for the run. Every launch therefore began with the offices you have checked out labelled "me", and relabelled with your name a few seconds later once the first feed poll came back.
  • Going to bed is something the body does, not something the picture does to it. The sequence lived in a gallery tile as a timeline of its own, which is worth nothing: a debugger with its own animation can look right while the station looks wrong, which is exactly what happened.
  • Every bed, not just the one in the picture. The couch learned to be stood beside rather than walked into, and the bunk was left easing to the middle of its mattress, so a body went to bed by walking into it. It stands a shin's reach out from the bunk while it is on its feet or sitting on the edge, and is on the mattress only once it is lying on it — the same rule the couch follows, from the same number.
  • A body stops where its feet go, not where its backside does. It walked to the middle of the seat and sat down there, which put it inside the couch on the way in and inside the mattress on the way to bed. A sitter's feet stay on the spot it stood on and the rest of it goes back behind them, so the spot to walk to is the seat's edge: the feet stop there, and sitting lands the body on the seat behind them.
  • A sitter's feet stay where it was standing. The body sat squarely on the spot with its shins reaching out in front of it, so standing up had to drag the legs back in under the torso, which is not how anybody gets out of a chair. The shins reach forward, so the body sits that far back: the feet keep the spot, and standing is nothing but the way back, the torso rising over the feet rather than the feet sliding under the torso.
  • It sits on the bunk, not beside it. The spot it sat on was a half-width past the mattress edge, so it perched in the air in front of the bed with nothing under it. A bunk is 0.34 across; sitting a little inside that edge puts the body on the mattress and its legs over the side, which is where they belong on the way in and on the way out.
  • It walks to the bed forwards. The two facings were the wrong way round, so it approached the bunk looking back over its shoulder at the door it came through, and left facing the way it had come.
  • Going to bed, as it is actually done. A bunk is come at from the side, not from the end: the body walks up to the edge, turns its back on the bed, sits down on it, and swings round into the bed's line as it stretches out. Getting up is the same moves in the opposite order — it swings back out of that line onto the edge, stands, and walks off the way it is already facing. Neither half has a move the other lacks, which is what makes them look like one thing done twice.
  • Nobody gets up off their back straight onto their feet. The rise was one movement and it read as a felled tree standing back up: a rigid box pivoting about its foot, no legs, no sitting, and it ended up standing on the mattress. The comment over it claimed it sat up first, which the code had never done.
  • The picture catches up to the facts whether or not the frame has time for the trimmings. Drawing a minion did two unrelated things under one name: it copied what the body is onto the figure — its pose, where it stands, how solid it is — and it added the flourishes on top, the shower's drops, the hop, the little routine that says what it is up to. A frame that had spent itself skipped both, so the figure went on showing the last frame's facts until a frame finally ran, and then jumped to catch up.
  • A body getting up is drawn getting up. The scene skipped posing a figure held still, which is reasonable for the one case that rule was written for — stepping out of a shuttle, where the body is halfway through a door and nothing should touch it — and exactly wrong for the other. Rousing a sleeper opens a moment for it to stand up in, and the scene spent that moment not drawing it standing up: the figure lay flat and still, and the rise began the instant the moment ended, alongside the walk it was supposed to come before.
  • A body getting to its feet is not lying down. Rousing cleared the nap and the bed, but a sleeper is flat because its activity is sleeping and it is in the quarters with nowhere to go, and none of that changed — so the body went on counting as lying for the whole of the moment it was given to stand up in. Nothing moved, because nothing had been told to. Then the moment ran out, the walk began, the path stopped being empty, and only then did the pose change: the body rose as it slid away, which is what it has looked like all evening.
  • A test for standing up before walking off. The rule is easy to state and was easy to break twice in an evening: a body roused from its bed holds where it lies until it is on its feet, and only then goes. The test puts a body to sleep in the quarters, sends it to the lounge, and asks for all three — that it was roused, that it stays within a twentieth of a tile while it rises, and that it arrives afterwards.
  • Getting to its feet is not a refusal. `wakeUntil` held a body still while it stepped out of a shuttle, and a command offered to a body in that state is turned away — sensibly, since it is halfway through a door. Rousing a sleeper borrowed the same field, so the order that woke it was refused by the very stillness it had just caused, and the morning never sent anyone to the couch.
  • A sleeper gets to its feet before it goes. Lying down is worked out from the bed, the nap and the place, and every path that gives a sleeping body something else to do clears one of those three first: sending it somewhere drops the nap before a step is planned, an errand names the room it is going to before it walks. By the time the walk was worked out the body was not lying any more, so nothing asked it to stand, and it slid off across the floor still flat on its back and stood up somewhere along the way.
  • The hover row dimmed the moment a minion set off. It asked whether the order in hand was a rest, and a turn in the gym is not one, so from the instant a minion accepted "off to the gym" every icon went grey — including the one that would have sent it back to the couch. The simulation would have allowed it: walking to the gym is a walk, and a walk can be turned round.
  • A body is in one pose, not three. Standing, sat and flat on the back were three booleans with a setter each, and every one of them called `removeAllActions` on the body and then animated it to its own idea of where it should be. The tick called all three in turn, so a body on the bench — which is both sat on a seat and flat on its back — ran two of them against each other and the call order decided which won.
  • A seat has its own height, and a body sits at it. There was one height for sitting, named for the bowl, and a couch is lower, so the moment the couch was given the sit its sitters hovered two centimetres above it. The prop carried 0.18 as a literal of its own and the pose carried 0.2, and nothing held the two together.
  • The gallery gets a tile for sitting. It already had one for sleeping and rising, a figure laid on a bed and put through the move on a loop with no station and no clock behind it, which is how a pose is meant to be looked at: put where you want it, doing what you want, in a few seconds. Sitting had no such tile, because until today only the bowl sat and nobody had needed to see it beside anything.
  • A couch is for sitting on. The sit was written once and used once: a visit to the bowl shortened the torso, put the legs out, moved the face down the box and eased the body onto the seat, while a lounger with nothing to do was drawn standing on its couch, the pose never asked for. `setSeated` was general all along — an offset and a seat height, nothing about plumbing — so the couch only ever had to ask.
  • Lying down is something a body is doing, not something it remembers. It was two stored flags kept in step by hand: the sleeping rule and the bench rule each set them when their own branch happened to run, and nothing set them back when a different order came, so the last value stood. That is what `dropLeftovers` was for, and why the list had to be added to every time a pose was invented — a hand-kept list of things to forget, which forgets silently.
  • One question about whether a body is free, asked in one place. Four pickers spelled it out inline — deliveries, carries, ordering a pallet and taking one over — and no two spelled it the same. The differences read as oversights rather than decisions, and inline filters four files apart cannot be compared by eye, so they drifted: carries alone would hand a crate to a teammate's stand-in, or to the minion inspecting the deck, since QA is not a job and nothing else stood in the way; and taking over a pallet would rouse somebody in the bath, though ordering one would not.
  • Nobody lies down at the crate. A body woken for a carry keeps the activity and the place it was sleeping under: the carry scheduler sets neither, unlike the pallet errand which says where it is going, and the leftovers an interrupting order drops restore the place for the bath and the gym but not for the quarters. So a carrier that had been asleep still answered to "asleep, in the quarters" when it reached the crate, and the moment it stood still there — no path, settled — the sleeping rule laid it down on the floor of the yard. What followed was the lying pose dragged along by the haul.
  • The separate-worlds path goes: it was never once taken. `Theme.separateWorlds` was a constant false with no theme overriding it, unlike the `padGap` beside it, so everything it guarded was unreachable from the day it was written — the four-hundred-unit world layout in `Fleet.arrange()`, the ground drawn once per station, the camera's whole-fleet frame giving way to one world at a time, and the `view.world` default remembering which world that was between launches.
  • A repository taken off the station is off the network too. The two switches could disagree: `shared(repo:)` asked only whether the box was ticked, never whether the repository was on the floor at all, so Hidden with Share left on went on being broadcast to the neighbours — taken off your own station because you did not want to look at it, and still told to everyone on the wire. There were two notions of hidden besides, the explicit override and the one `station(cwd:owner:repo:)` works out for a private repository with the private station off, and the call sites disagreed about which they meant. Now `shown(repo:)` answers it once and sharing and teammates both ask it.
  • The menu bar says what kind of thing each item is. It was one menu doing four jobs at once: what the application is, where the camera points, the tools for working on rumkapsel itself, and writing in about a bug, all in a single list under the app's own name. Now each has its own: the application menu keeps About, updates, settings and the way out; View holds the camera and the two toggles worth a key; Station holds its dealings with GitHub; Develop holds the gallery and the simulator, out of the ordinary path but always there; and Help holds the two ways of writing in.
  • The front belongs to whoever is at the keyboard. Both halves of it were the wrong way round: a build asked for by hand opened with `open -g` and arrived behind the window being worked in, while a scripted render opened the simulator with `makeKeyAndOrderFront` and `activate(ignoringOtherApps:)` and took the screen from whatever was there. So `./build.sh run` now simply opens, because a build waited for is one worth looking at; and a run started by a script rather than by a person orders its windows in behind and leaves the front alone. The one thing that decides this is `Scripted.run`, which the activation policy already reasoned about on its own further down the file and can now be read by anything that opens a window.
  • A pallet measures the way ahead rather than assuming it. It was the one moving solid on the floor that never asked what stood in front of it: bodies walk round the obstacle grid and plan again when a walk is spoilt, but the slab took its legs from the arithmetic of the rows, drew them once as it set off, and crept along them to the end however the yard changed behind it. The way out is measured now against what stands this instant, the whole band the plate sweeps, aisles tried nearest the doorway first; and every step is measured before the plate is moved over it, not after. A crate in the way means hands off and a fresh way worked out from where it stands, a body in the way only means holding the leg until they have walked on, since they will and a crate will not. Boxed in, it asks again each second and goes no further after thirty, the crates coming off where it stands as they already do when a dispatcher wanders off mid-errand.
  • The dispatcher carries a tablet to the storage console, not a clipboard. A clipboard is not what anyone would reach for to order a pallet today, and the tablet is already in the hands of everyone coding, reading and writing, so the errand borrows it until the pallet operation is given a look of its own
  • A staging pallet floats where nothing else stands, and nothing walks through it. The slab is four crates across and two deep, so it fits the single cell of aisle a yard leaves between its crate rows; storage keeps the lane through its doorway clear, in front because the way out must be open and behind because that is where the pusher puts its hands on it; and a yard block is six columns rather than four, since four gave half its crate cells to that lane and left one stride to get past the slab. A crate that reaches storage while the pallet is still standing there is lifted aboard too rather than left behind on the rows. Walks are planned round the pallet where it floats this instant, not where the obstacle grid last saw it, and a walk whose line crosses it is planned again at once
  • A minion holds its tablet the way a person does. The slab hinged off the visor, near edge high at the nose and the screen falling away toward the floor, because a positive pitch about X drops the far edge; it now pitches the other way and hangs a little lower, so the near edge tucks in at the belly, the far edge lifts outwards and up, and the glowing face comes back to meet the head. Every activity that reaches for the tablet — coding, reading, writing, qa, planning, a skill, and a lounger on the couch — shares the one slab and picks up the new angle
  • The Space Center's input and output are set pieces, not tinted cells. The launch complex is poured as one kerbed apron with screening at the hatch, the store, the test rows and the pad painted on it, a white line round the pad, a flame trench under where a rocket stands, a service gantry with its arm swung over it and floodlights on the pad's outer corners; the bay is an apron outside the hull with a box painted where each ship sets down, and the airlock the marked passage running back in through it. A slab is one sampling of the distance to a run of cells, cut at its edge, so a set of them is one shape; drawn inward it measures to the ring of cells outside the set instead, since the distance to the set's own squares says only how deep one square is and would cut every cell into a lozenge of its own
  • The Cape is keyed to the ground it stands on, not to how far the fleet reaches. Space Center's world was drawn from the fleet's bounding box and a running seed, so opening an office moved the coastline and reshuffled every palm and rock on the map. Now each patch of ground belongs to the station whose floor lies nearest, and what grows on it follows from that station's own cell: the same tuft, the same size, the same way about, wherever the fleet has grown to. The sea is cut by marching squares from one sampling of the distance to a wandering shoreline, four levels off it, so the water's edge curves into bays and headlands with shallows, foam and sand behind it, where lawn and sea were two rectangles with a ruled row of bank tiles between them. Palms stand in groves along the sand and scrub gathers in thickets over the lawn, both thinning to open ground between, rather than an even speckle over everything
  • A look may give minions tools of their own and draw a message its own way, and say whether working one throws sparks. The scene asks the look before it builds the hammer, the scanner, the torch, the tablet, the clipboard and the telekinesis wand, and binds the swing, the aim and the wand's tip and light by name, so a look's own tool moves the way the classic one does
  • The HUD reads the look's background and inks itself dark on a light ground, so repo names, counts, the log and the status stay legible on grass; THEMES.md names every hook as it now is, the set pieces, worlds, tile context, launch and Shapes, and what a look still cannot do
  • Shapes: flat organic shapes for a look. A field is sampled once over a rectangle and cut at any number of levels into flat meshes by marching squares, a row's run of full cells merged into one quad, so coastlines, clearings, yards and paths have soft edges instead of the grid's; a tile's patch runs on into its owner's neighbours and is cached by which of the eight they are; and Noise, keyed to world position, keeps a world where it was when the station round it grows. A run with no window draws no world at all, so a look's ground never slows the gate
  • Looks follow the layers of a place. The protocol is ordered by them, the world, the input, the output, the center, the idle areas and the growth zone, and gains what the layers need: a look may draw the bay and the airlock, or decon, storage, the deck and the pad, whole as a set piece while the scene keeps the doors, the hatch, the console and every spot; it may hide a floor's square plane while the tile still names, dims and unfolds its detail; a tile's detail is told which of its eight neighbours share its owner; and a rocket leaves the way the look says. Under a theme of separate worlds each station is laid a world's gap from the next and the camera frames one at a time, switched with the station keys and the menu, cut to rather than flown to, and remembered. RK_DEMO_OFFICES adds offices to the demo to see a theme under load
  • THEMES.md: stations are worlds, shown one at a time, the private station a world of its own rather than a site in a shared landscape or a quarter of one place; moving between worlds is still to design
  • THEMES.md: how to design a theme. The six layers of a place (the input and the output as fixed set pieces, the center that says what the place is, idle areas as scenery, the growth zone, the world around it), stations as sites, designing for change, how theme work is judged against its references and across growth, where a theme lives in the code, what a look cannot do yet, and what the first medieval attempts taught. The README points to it
  • A look can tell an office from the rooms every station has: a tile's floor kind gains fixed, for the lounge, the dorm, the bath and the gym, where they counted as offices
  • A theme names the station's parts and doings in its own words: floor signs, hover text, orders and log lines read from a vocabulary on the theme, Classic's by default, and a theme changes only the words it draws as something else. Every test run pins Classic's words, since the scenarios expect log lines by what they say
  • The fixed rooms' furniture comes from the look: the lounge, the bath, the gym and the beds, with the classic pieces as the default. A look hands back its pieces placed as the room stands, the solid ones and the fixtures apart, and the towel, the bar and the bag the scene moves; the scene names them as before, and a gym without a bar or a bag is simply not animated
  • Every requirement of a look has a default, the classic station's, so a look says only what it changes: ClassicLook is empty, and the Kenney looks keep their overrides and fall back on the Classic pieces where a model is missing, where each kept a ClassicLook of its own to ask
  • A look may draw a ship's path. A flight says how far through its phase it is, which slot it serves and which side it leaves toward, and the scene asks the look for a position and a heading before it falls back on the simulation's own path, which still says when a ship comes and onto which slot it lands
  • The airlock runs five tiles through the hull and the bay hangs outside its far end, in every look, so the hatch is the station's edge and the bay no longer sits against it. The bay, its landing slots and the carriers' stands move out with the passage; a leaver cycles at the inner door, walks the passage and fades from the hatch on, where it faded as soon as the cycle ended. Layouts are saved as fleet-v22, since saved hallway and offices may stand where the passage now runs. --layout-tests holds, for every theme, that nothing else stands in the airlock or the bay and that the bay touches the station only at the hatch
  • A look is told what kind of floor a tile is and what lies past each walled edge, and may drop the dark lines between owners. Kit, the Kenney model loader, moves to a file of its own, and the spots a look dresses — the pad's free corners, the parking beside the bay, an office's outer wall — are shared by any look that wants them. Decon floor has an owner like the rest of the yard, where every edge of it counted as open ground
  • Themes live behind a Look: the scene asks the current look for every drawn piece and no longer branches on which theme is on. Theme is model-only (title, credit, and padGap, the one knob a theme turns on the plan); Looks/ holds the protocol, ClassicLook moved over as it was, and KenneyLook with its kit loader and ground, falling back to the classic piece when a model is missing. The layout tests pin Classic and run the yard checks for every theme; the settings credit names the Nature Kit too
  • Shared stations converge. A peer's office is adopted where the peer put it: on free floor beside our hallway as before, and now also with the shortest dig through free floor to reach it, up to twelve tiles, where it used to be placed afresh and drift. When both machines placed the same room before hearing each other, the lower peer name's cells stand: every such room is cleared at once, since one often stands where another of theirs belongs, then theirs are adopted; hallway we dug under their floor is given back if what remains is one piece from the plaza with every door kept. The plan's own arms and alleys are never given back. --layout-tests holds two stations that placed one room differently to agreeing once the lower name's cells are taken, the hallway still whole and every room still with a door
  • The kit's earth is an orange that reads as a prop from across the lawn, a rock passing for the bath's towel: sand on the shore, stone on the rocks
  • Two snapshots of the demo, one a theme, for the pull request and the README to point at
  • A second look for the station, picked under Settings › General › Look: Kenney Space Center, the same floor plan on the ground as the Cape has it. Astronauts for minions, hung from the body's middle so every pose carries them; the kit's platforms on every tile, kerbed only where the floor meets the grass; arches on the airlock and the decon hatch; a comms tower with a turning dish for the monolith; kit rockets sized as before with the hatch and flame by name, speeders for the shuttles, a desk in every office, fuel by the pad and a rover in the bay. A lawn to every side and the sea past the yard, a bank of the Nature Kit's tiles along the shore with palms up it and scrub on the grass, the greens retinted from the kit's turquoise. On the ground the pad stands five tiles out from the deck on a two-lane causeway toward the water, and the view starts turned about so the pad faces right. Classic is untouched; the theme is a config field and a switch rebuilds the fleet. The models used (CC0) live in Resources/Kenney and build.sh copies them into the bundle
  • The frame rate stays at 30 whenever the window can be seen, focused or not: a desk toy sits beside the work, and dropping to 8 the moment it lost focus made it lag in the corner of the eye. Only a covered or hidden window goes to 8
  • The plan draws its dead-end alleys off the long arms again, every few runs, two or three tiles, on the side the arm last jogged away from, reserved like the arms and dug whole when a room wants the frontage; the passages between arms stay demand-dug. Judged on the forty and eighty room fills (RK_FILL=1 prints both, with mean walk, loops and footprint), that gives the crinkle back and a tighter footprint at the same mean walk.
